speakeroldname: Mr. W. H. GOLDING (Huron Perth) moved:
subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST AND SECOND REPORTS
speechtext: That the first and second reports of standing committee on standing orders, presented on May 14, be now concurred in.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST AND SECOND REPORTS
speechtext:
I object to this motion. I think the members of the House of Commons ought to understand its import before it is passed. By a

Standing Orders
recent order of the house the committee was instructed to study the request of a certain insurance company which desired to have a refund made to it of some S700, and the committee, on that reference, brought in this report. The committee has not given the house adequate reasons why these funds, which are paid legally under the rules of the house, should be refunded to the company. The rules provide that certain payments shall be made on the incorporation of a company

so many hundred dollars on account of the capitalization-and* if the petition is late in being introduced to parliament a penalty is imposed. The payment was made last year. The company was not before parliament in time. For some reason or other which is not apparent, the bill did not pass the House of Commons. It has been reintroduced, and they suggest now that the whole fee paid last year, legally and in accordance with the rules of the house, be refunded to them. The strange part of it is they suggest in this report that the penalty of $300 should be repaid not to the company but to a private individual.
I suggest to the Minister of Finance that he had better look into the matter. What are the rules there for, and why should moneys be refunded without adequate reason? Four hundred dollars was paid and the penalty was paid under the rules of the house for failure to be on time. They ask that the whole thing be refunded and that $300 be given to a private individual, which in principle is wrong.
I see no reason why there should be a refund of any portion of this money. If the company was late in getting into parliament last year and now seeks to carry the bill through, it should do so without the public revenues suffering. We are getting pretty free with remissions in this house and I think the whole position should be reviewed. I would ask the Minister of Finance to review the whole matter. The company is the Alliance Insurance company. I do not know anything about the company, but the strange part of the whole request and recommendation is that the $300 paid as a penalty shall be refunded to a private individual, the solicitor in charge of the bill.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN FIRST AND SECOND REPORTS
speechtext: I am satisfied to let the matter stand.

subtopic: APPRECIATION OP RESPONSF, OP CANADIAN PEOPLE IN EXCEEDING OBJECTIVE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: APPRECIATION OP RESPONSF, OP CANADIAN PEOPLE IN EXCEEDING OBJECTIVE
speechtext:
I should like to take the earliest opportunity to place on record the government's appreciation of the splendid response of the Canadian people to the appeal for the fourth victory loan. When, on the 15th of this month, the period fixed for the campaign had terminated the objective of $1,100 million had been exceeded by over $100 million. As soon as the official returns of the campaign are available the Minister of Finance will of course indicate them to the house.
What is even more significant than the fact that the total objective was oversubscribed is that reports indicate that the objective of $500,000,000 for the general canvass and payroll subscriptions will also be exceeded. That fact in itself is a magnificent demonstration of the patriotism of the men and women of Canada, and an equally emphatic evidence of national unity of purpose in firm support of Canada's fighting men in the campaigns which must be undertaken before victory can be achieved.
I should like to express the government's thanks to the chairman of the national war finance committee, Mr. G. W. Spinney, and to the thousands of devoted Canadians _ in national, provincial and local organizations without whose untiring efforts the loan could not have succeeded. I am sure all hon. memr-bers would wish to share in this expression of appreciation of the services of the men and women of our country and of those from other lands who have given of their talents, time and energies to this phase of Canada's war effort. Speaking for the government, may I also express appreciation of the -contribution to the success of the campaign made by hon. members of all parties in their own constituencies and elsewhere.
Hon. members, I am sure, will feel that I am justified in extending warm congratulations to the Minister of Finance, whose efforts on behalf of the loan have been indefatigable. He is entitled to the sense of deep satisfaction which he must be experiencing to-day. The confidence he expressed in the Canadian people in setting the high objective of the Fourth victory loan has been more than fulfilled.
In expressing appreciation of the support and determination of the people of Canada, there is one word I should like to add. The completeness of the victory in North Africa is causing some persons who ought to know better, to say that the major issue in the
Fourth Victory Loan

war in Europe has been decided, and that we may look for the end of the war this year. Significant as is the North African victory, I am sure that in Europe the heaviest fighting still lies ahead. Further decisive battles have still to be fought and won. We have not yet reached the moment of supreme ordeal. The *vay in which the Canadian people have responded to the victory Joan shows that they have not allowed any false optimism concerning an early victory to weaken their' will. We know it would be fatal to let one victory destroy our sense of proportion. The victory in Africa has only touched the fringes of axis power; the assault on Europe has not yet begun. There remains as well the task of defeating Japan. This, clearly, is not a time for relaxing, but a time for redoubling our efforts. It is a time for strengthening our hearts and minds for the tremendous exertions which will still be required to bring the cause of freedom to the hour of victory.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: APPRECIATION OP RESPONSF, OP CANADIAN PEOPLE IN EXCEEDING OBJECTIVE
speechtext: I should like to add my words to the congratulatory terms in which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) described the response of the Canadian people to the fourth victory loan. I should like also to support the warning the right hon. gentleman gave with respect to our position having regard to the entire theatre of the war, and to caution the people, as he has done, against any over-optimistic trend at this time. I should like as well to say to the government that in this fourth victory loan the people have done their part. The responsibility now rests with the administration to see that the money thus subscribed is expended with the least waste and the least inefficiency that government operation can possibly achieve.

subtopic: APPRECIATION OP RESPONSF, OP CANADIAN PEOPLE IN EXCEEDING OBJECTIVE
speechtext:
We should like to join in congratulating the Minister of Finance and the country generally on the satisfactory outcome of the loan.
I am sure we are all gratified at the result.

subtopic: APPRECIATION OP RESPONSF, OP CANADIAN PEOPLE IN EXCEEDING OBJECTIVE
speechtext: I feel, too, Mr. Speaker, that there is cause for deep satisfaction throughout the country, and particularly in the heart of the Minister of Finance, because of the success of the fourth victory loan. It was a great effort, and it has been crowned with great success.

subtopic: CANADIAN MINISTER TO WASHINGTON-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. COLDWELL IN DEBATE ON MAY 14

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADIAN MINISTER TO WASHINGTON-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. COLDWELL IN DEBATE ON MAY 14
speechtext:
I should like to refer to

a statement made by the hon. leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group (Mr. Coldwell) on Friday last. I regret that I was unavoidably engaged elsewhere at the time and so did not hear the statement when it was made. The remarks to which I wrish to draw particular attention will be found at page 2680 of Hansard for May 14, 1943.
The Prime Minister has announced that he is going to Washington. I think it would be well for him while there to inquire into all the matters concerning the signing of Canada's agreement; for I want to ask him what part in this agreement and in the general agreement we are discussing under this bill the Department of External Affairs played. What part did it play in relation to this country?
The matter to which my hon,. friend was referring was the Shipshaw development. So far as the Department of External Affairs is concerned, it had nothing whatever to do with any of the arrangements with respect to the Shipshaw power development. In reply to a request from the United States government, formal assurance was given by the government of Canada, through the Department of External Affairs, to the United States government that there would be no restriction of any kind on the export from Canada to the United States of "all Canadian aluminum purchased by the Metals Reserve Company under contracts entered into prior to the termination of the present war." This, so far as the Department of External Affairs was concerned, was wholly a matter of formal procedure.
When I read the statement of my hon. friend and saw that it contained numerous reflections upon the Canadian minister to Washington, the Honourable Leighton McCarthy, I directed the Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs to have a copy of the statement made by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party sent immediately to Mr. McCarthy in order that he might have these representations before him. That was done on Saturday, and yesterday the under-secretary received from Mr. McCarthy a statement which I think answers all the points' raised1 by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, which statement I wish to read to the house:
Questions asked by Mr. Coldwell may be summarized as follows:
(I)	"I want to ask him what part in this agreement and in the general agreement we are discussing under this bill the Department of External Affairs played. What part did it play in relation to this country?"
Answer:	So far as the minister in charge
of this legation is concerned, the answer to this question is that he played no part whatever, and he goes further and says that he has

Washington Legation
never discussed with any member of the United States administration or officer thereof, the question of supply of aluminum or the subject matter of the agreements referred to.
Nor has he discussed any questions of taxation with any member of the United States or Canadian administrations or officials thereof.
(2)	Mr. Coldwell says: "I find it very difficult to believe that the minister at Washington had nothing to do with negotiations in regard to these matters involving Canada and the United States."
Answer: No matter how difficult Mr. Coldwell finds it to believe, the fact is that the minister had nothing whatever to do with these negotiations, and played no part in them.
(3)	Mr. Coldwell says: "He (Mr. McCarthy) is still a director and vice-president of the parent company, the Aluminum Company of the United States."
Answer: Mr. McCarthy is not now nor has he ever been a director or vice-president or officer of the Aluminum Company of America.
(4)	Mr. Coldwell: "As a matter of fact Mr. McCarthy has been for thirty years legal consultant to the Aluminum Company of Canada."
Answer: That would be a correct statement beginning with the year 1907, but incorrect as to the last probably 8 or 10 years, when he was superseded by Mr. Aime Geoffrion, K.C., of Montreal, who has been elected a director of Aluminum Company of Canada in Mr. McCarthy's place.
Mr. J. P. Van-Lane referred to by Mr. Coldwell has been a director of the Aluminum Company of Canada for a great many years.
(5)	Mr. Coldwell: "Mr. McCarthy is a director of a number of power companies, which, like the Aluminum Company group, have used every means possible to prevent the development of public power in this country, particularly St. Lawrence power."
Answer: Mr. McCarthy is a director of only one power company, namely, the Saguenay Power Company. It is absolutely untrue to say that he has used any means to prevent the development of public power in Canada, particularly St. Lawrence power.
(6)	Mr. Coldwell:	"Personally I think Mr. McCarthy should be asked to come back to Canada and explain to the government why it is that he has retained these directorates in spite of custom."
Answer:	There is no necessity for Mr. McCarthy to go back to Canada to explain this. The Prime Minister was told by Mr. McCarthy before he accepted the Washington position that he would not dissociate himself from his business connections, and that if it were necessary for him to do so he would have to decline to take the Washington post.
It might be pointed out here that the acceptance by Mr. McCarthy of the Washington post was of a temporary character, pending the convalescence of Mr. Loring Christie, who remained minister, and Mr. McCarthy declined even to say that he would remain for the duration of the war.
Mr. King in making the announcement stated as follows:
"He has agreed to accept the position for such time as he is able to give his services at Washington."
Newspapers at the time this announcement was made all fully reported Mr. McCarthy's various directorates, and the public were fully aware of his business associations.
Mr. Coldwell, apparently, from Hansard, was in the house at the time Mr. King made his announcement of Mr. McCarthy's acceptance of this post, and could hardly have been unaware of what the newspapers were carrying in regard to Mr. McCarthy and his business associations.
(7)	Mr. Coldwell states: "This house should know that the New York State power authorities in its annual report for 1937 named Mr. McCarthy as one of the men blocking the development of the St. Lawrence waterways as a public enterprise."
Answer: Mr. McCarthy never heard of this alleged report until a few weeks ago when referred to by Mr. Stone, correspondent for the New York newspaper P.M., from whom Mr. Coldwell evidently got this quotation. Mr. McCarthy told Mr. Stone that it was absolutely incorrect. However, he passed it on to Mr. Coldwell, and Mr. Coldwell has seen fit to use it.
Mr. McCarthy specifically states that he is not one of those *who opposes the development of the water power resources in the St. Lawrence and Niagara rivers, but on the contrary was one of' those who supported it, and is prepared to support it either by public enterprise or private enterprise. He denies explicitly that he ever played any part in obstructing development of these waterways by either public or private enterprise.
I have only to add that I am prepared to support all the representations made by Mr. McCarthy in the statement he has presented here. What is disclosed with respect to his relationships with the government, and his position at Washington, are entirely in accord with my knowledge of the situation.
As Mr. McCarthy says, at the time he took the position in Washington it was only as a result of very strong persuasion, both on my part and on the part of some of my colleagues, that he, as a patriotic duty, undertook for the time being to give up the active associations he had with different businesses in Canada, and to give his entire time at Washington to the service of our country, while serving there in the position of minister. It has been with real difficulty that it has been possible to persuade Mr. McCarthy to continue in that position. In 1941 he asked me if, in the light of conditions then existing, he might not be relieved of the post, and someone else be appointed in his place. In 1942 he went so far as to tender his resignation, but I persuaded him to remain, having knowledge of the exceptional services he was rendering not only to Canada but as well to other parts of the British empire, through his post at Washington as Canadian minister. It would have been deplorable had he not seen his way clear to continue in that position.
Washington Legation

In February of this year Mr. McCarthy delivered an address, before the Canadian Club at Toronto, I believe it was. In that address, which was broadcast, he made it perfectly clear that he was not clinging to the job he now holds, but that the job was clinging to him; and that he wished it to be known that his continuation in the position he held at Washington was due entirely to his sense of public duty, and as a result of the request the government had made that he continue in that position.
I wish it were possible for me to give to the house some of the communications which have passed between Mr. McCarthy and myself in regard to what he has achieved in his work at Washington. Unfortunately time and other circumstances do not permit my doing so. But I do say to the house I have the best of reasons for knowing that Mr. McCarthy is performing a duty as minister for Canada at Washington which, I believe, under existing circumstances, and under conditions of war, could not be as well performed by any other person who could have been selected.
May I say a word with respect to resignations from directorates, and the like, by one who does not seek to make the diplomatic service a career. Mr. McCarthy has never sought to be a diplomat. He has had an exceptionally wide business experience, and has an exceptional acquaintance with men in all parts of this continent; and those same exceptional relationships are of service to the country in the position he now holds. But it would not be possible to secure for diplomatic posts for the period of the war men of Mr. McCarthy's attainments in business and in professional life if appointees were obliged1 to sever completely all their business associations and connections. I do not believe hon. members think that any gentleman who has honourable obligations, when he is holding the high position of minister in another country, is likely to descend to any act which would be open to criticism, or one which would not be expected from a person holding that position.
I knew Mr. McCarthy in the days when he was a member of the house-a good many years ago-as at least some other hon. members who are here now also knew him. I am quite sure that they will agree with all his friends that a man of higher integrity, a man who would be more scrupulous in the observance of all that is essential in public relations, could not be found anywhere. I expect to see Mr. McCarthy to-morrow, and I have no doubt that as a result of what has been said by the leader of -the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation I shall again have to

use what persuasive powers I have to cause him to continue to carry on in the position which he has filled so admirably. However, I believe he will be the first to appreciate that, in the light of -the statement which he himself has made, innuendoes of the character made by the hon. member are really unworthy of him. Knowing the appreciation my hon. friend has of what is involved in these diplomatic relations, I cannot understand why he did not do what Mr. Stone did- in relation to Mr. McCarthy, and go direct to Mr. McCarthy to see if he would be justified in making these representations in public. My hon. friend could have come to me and asked if these things were true, and I would have told him. If men who assume high responsibilities of -this character are to be subjected to all kinds of irresponsible representations it will not be possible for the government to keep in the public service the men who are so greatly needed in this time of war.

subtopic: CANADIAN MINISTER TO WASHINGTON-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. COLDWELL IN DEBATE ON MAY 14
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know under what order of business this is being done, but since the statement I made on Friday has been criticized and attacked by the Prime Minister I presume I have a right as a matter of privilege to say something in relation to it.
I am glad -to have any correction of any misstatement that I may have made, but what I said was said in perfectly good faith and was based on information which I believed to be correct. The Prime Minister has not dealt with the very important statement which I made in connection with Mr. McCarthy, that is, that right up to January of this year he was a director of the Aluminum Company of Canada. If I were in error in speaking of his association with the Aluminum Company of the United States, I was not in error with regard to the Aluminum Company of Canada. I made this statement because I believed, as I have always believed, that Canada should be represented, abroad by gentlemen who have no association with companies or corporations which may be involved in negotiations between our country and the ones to which -they represent us. I understand that it is obligatory upon cabinet ministers to resign directorships. I understand that when Mr. Burchell was appointed high commissioner -to Australia a few years ago special permission was given to him to retain a directorship when he was acting in that capacity. I bring this to the attention of the house because I believe, in spite of what the Prime Minister has said, as I stated in my remarks on Friday, that while Mr. McCarthy may have been guilty of nothing improper, this is an unhealthy situa-

Coal Emergency
tion and I think it is a matter which the government should take into consideration. They should see to it that when we are negotiating deals of this description with other countries which may involve great corporations our ministers are free from any association which may lead to the kind of suspicion which was in my mind and in the minds of a good many other people.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADIAN MINISTER TO WASHINGTON-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. COLDWELL IN DEBATE ON MAY 14
speechtext:
In reference to the statement my hon. friend has made, this is the answer which Mr. McCarthy himself has made to the hon. member:
Mr. Coldwell:	"As a matter of fact Mr. McCarthy has been for thirty years legal consultant to the Aluminum Company of Canada."
Answer: That would be a correct statement beginning with the year 1907, but incorrect as to the last probably eight or ten years, when he was superseded by Mr. Aime Geoffrion, K.C., of Montreal, who has been elected a director of Aluminum Company of Canada in Mr. McCarthy's place.

subtopic: CANADIAN MINISTER TO WASHINGTON-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. COLDWELL IN DEBATE ON MAY 14
speechtext: Since when?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CANADIAN MINISTER TO WASHINGTON-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. COLDWELL IN DEBATE ON MAY 14
speechtext: Eight or ten years. He has been legal consultant for eight or ten years and was chosen a director later. May I say a word in reference to my hon. friend's further remarks about gentlemen who happen to be directors. Are we to assume in this parliament that when a gentleman takes on a public position as a war duty he is to be subjected to criticism as one who will be performing unworthy acts simply because he happens to have a business connection with some large concern? I do not think it is fair to human nature to assume anything of that kind. I believe that most men have a strong sense of public duty. If a man were entering a diplomatic career in which he expected to remain for the rest of his life, I agree that he should there and then have to choose between directorships and the like-

subtopic: CANADIAN MINISTER TO WASHINGTON-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. COLDWELL IN DEBATE ON MAY 14

subtopic: CANADIAN MINISTER TO WASHINGTON-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. COLDWELL IN DEBATE ON MAY 14
speechtext: My hon. friend says that cabinet ministers all have to give up their directorships.

subtopic: CANADIAN MINISTER TO WASHINGTON-REFERENCE TO REMARKS OF MR. COLDWELL IN DEBATE ON MAY 14

That has not been the practice; it is a matter which is left to the honour of the minister concerned. I have never requested a cabinet minister to give up any position which he was holding. I have always trusted to his sense of integrity and what he considered was the right and proper thing to do in the circumstances.

maintopic: ISSUE OF PROCLAMATION DECLARING EXISTENCE OF A STATE OF EMERGENCY

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ISSUE OF PROCLAMATION DECLARING EXISTENCE OF A STATE OF EMERGENCY
speechtext:
I desire to table order in council P.C. 4091, dated to-day, authorizing the issue of a proclamation declaring that a state of national emergency exists in regard to the production of coal in Canada. I think perhaps the order is sufficiently important for me to read to the house. It is as follows:
17th May, 1943.
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report dated May 17, 1943, from the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, the Prime Minister, representing:
That the Canadian economy and the national war effort based upon it depend upon adequate supplies of coal;
That the need for coal has grown and continues to grow with the development of the war effort;
That supplies of coal are substantially below the level required to meet the increased national needs resulting from the war; and
That, unless supplies of coal are forthwith increased and maintained at an adequate level the war effort and the life and health of the nation will be gravely imperilled.
The committee, therefore, on the recommendation of the Prime Minister, advise that a proclamation do issue declaring that a state of national emergency exists in regard to the production of coal in Canada.
A. I). P. Heeney,
Clerk of the Privy Council.
The action that will be taken by the government under this proclamation will be disclosed to the house at a subsequent sitting.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: ISSUE OF PROCLAMATION DECLARING EXISTENCE OF A STATE OF EMERGENCY
speechtext: Has the passing of this order in council any relation to the situation which evidently exists in the United States? What legal effect will the declaration of a state of emergency have so far as our coal production and our coal situation are concerned? What results may we expect to flow from the enact-* ment of this order in council?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ISSUE OF PROCLAMATION DECLARING EXISTENCE OF A STATE OF EMERGENCY
speechtext:
The proclamation is made regardless altogether of the situation which exists in the United States at the present time, but I want to make it perfectly clear that situation is one which the ministers of the crown must necessarily take into account as having certain possible consequences in relation to Canada's fuel supply. Apart from that situation there is the fact, to mention just one thing, that we are about a month late this year as compared with other years in the matter of the transportation of coal supplies. There has been a falling off in the production of coal for a long time past.
Coal Emergency

maintopic: ISSUE OF PROCLAMATION DECLARING EXISTENCE OF A STATE OF EMERGENCY
speechtext: In our own fields?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ISSUE OF PROCLAMATION DECLARING EXISTENCE OF A STATE OF EMERGENCY
speechtext: In our own fields. The war effort- itself is making extra demands on the coal of the country in the matter of transportation, in the -matter of supplies, and in the matter of what is required for the manufacture of munitions and other commodities. These are some of the reasons. As to the action that will be taken, the house will be informed a little later as to the precise action which will be taken by the government to help to meet the emergent situation we are facing. When I use the word "emergent" I am not using it in relation to what is happening to-day or may happen to-morrow; I am referring to the situation as it will develop in Canada unless we can overtake the falling off of supplies within the course of the next few months. We have to realize that there is an autumn and winter ahead of us and provision must be made as soon as possible. Then the house will have observed that when trouble threatened a few days ago in the United States, shipments of coal to Canada were immediately cut off. That may happen again, and no one can say what shortage there may be in the United States in their own supply if there is a serious stoppage of production in that country. All these facts being considered, the government have thought it advisable to take the action which it has taken.

maintopic: ISSUE OF PROCLAMATION DECLARING EXISTENCE OF A STATE OF EMERGENCY
speechtext: Has the mere passing of the order in council any legal effect? I think it will have to be followed up by other action. I hope that the public will be kept informed, because this is certainly an important matter. I wholly approve what the government has done. I think it should have been done before this.

maintopic: DEVELOPMENT OF PRODUCTION OF EASTERN MINES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: DEVELOPMENT OF PRODUCTION OF EASTERN MINES
speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister or the Minister of Mines and Resources whether any special investigation is being made of the capacity of coal mines, especially in eastern Canada, to increase their production and open up new areas. I have in mind particularly the locality of Thorbum, where there are millions of tons of coal which could be mined at a minimum initial expense. If investigations along this line were undertaken to encourage the operation of the mines and increased production, and to get the good-will of miners, a very considerable increase in tonnage could be obtained.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DEVELOPMENT OF PRODUCTION OF EASTERN MINES
speechtext: I cannot answer my hon. friend's question offhand, but it is one that possibly one of my colleagues might reply to a little later. I would say to my hon. friend and to other members of the house that the government will warmly welcome any suggestions which members may have to make with respect to ways and means by which the coal supply of Canada can be rapidly augmented.

maintopic: DEVELOPMENT OF PRODUCTION OF EASTERN MINES
speechtext: In order to clarify the situation, the order which has been tabled is merely a proclamation declaring an emergency in the fuel situation in Canada. I understand it will be followed by certain regulations designed to cure the situation. In view of the fact that the mining industry is unionized from coast to coast, I would ask the Prime Minister whether the representatives of the miners' unions have been called to consultation, or whether that will be done before any regulations affecting the industry are framed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DEVELOPMENT OF PRODUCTION OF EASTERN MINES
speechtext: The answer is yes.

PERDUE, SASK., POSTMASTERSHIP
speechtext:
1.	Is the position of postmaster at Perdue,

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: USE OF PRISONERS OF WAR FOR FARM LABOUR
speechtext:
The hon. member for Weybum
(Mr. Douglas) asked a question on Thursday last with reference to prisoners of war. I should like to make a statement in reply.
Use of Italian prisoners of war is being made in England on labour projects with satisfactory results, but almost all prisoners of war interned in this country are of German nationality, and the extent to which German prisoners may be successfully employed can only be determined from experience gained in the work projects initially undertaken.
The intention is that in initiating operations, the prisoners employed will be selected from those volunteering for employment and who are considered sufficiently reliable by the internment camp authorities for transfer to such employment and suitable for work on the employment project to be undertaken.
The men selected will be transferred by the military authorities to small labour detachments assigned for work. We expect these detachments will be housed in labour camps adjacent to, or within the area of, the labour project, or the area in which the detachment may operate, and in some instances, they will be housed in the main internment camp if the employment is within easy access of the camp.
The Department of Labour will assume responsibility to provide for the operation of the labour camps and the arrangements for employment. A limited number of military personnel will be attached to each detachment for disciplinarian purposes, but the responsibility for the labour detachments will be assumed by the Department of Labour.
The nature of the labour projects undertaken will necessarily be such as will involve the employment of a minimum personnel to supervise the employment and to provide reasonable assurances for the security and discipline of the prisoners employed.
Wood cutting and mining work and selected types of agricultural work appear to offer the most suitable opportunities for employment. Projects providing suitable employment and

Supply
for which camp facilities are available or can be supplied with little added cost will receive favourable consideration at the outset.
Notwithstanding- the careful selection of prisoners, hon. members will recognize that greater risks of escape must be accepted in placing these prisoners in useful employment than are involved in their detention in internment camp.
Canada is a party to the prisoners of war convention concluded at Geneva in 1929, so that the conditions of employment and rates of pay and provision for welfare of prisoners of war provided in this country will conform to the terms of the convention, and also be in conformity with British practices in this regard.
The appointment of officers to have charge of the administration of this matter will be made at an early day, and every effort will be made to expedite the initiation of labour projects. Hon. members will realize that the initiation of particular projects inevitably will be delayed somewhat, and that it will be necessary to develop plans gradually and follow practices dictated by the experience we gain as we go along.

short appropriation act providing $648,333,333.33, being one-sixth of $3,890,000,000 which was the amount of the resolution originally placed on the order paper. I will send these up to you, Mr. Speaker, and I hope they will go through promptly. Perhaps we had better take the non-war appropriation first.

Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, I am very glad indeed to consent to the bills suggested by the minister being put through, and that the supply should be one-sixth, though I would not want this to be a precedent. However, that is not my purpose in rising. On going into supply I have the right to raise any grievance. I was surprised this afternoon when the Prime Minister made his statement with regard to an alleged misstatement by myself. I sent out and got a copy of the "Survey of Corporate Securities" for 1942, in which I find that Aluminium Limited is the parent company; apparently on Friday, when I made my statement, I included the words "of the United States." Then I find this: "Owns all outstanding stock of Aluminum Company of Canada Limited-"
What is the hon. gentleman reading from?

From the "Survey of Corporate Securities" for 1942, the report on Aluminium Limited-the latest authority I can get.
Owns all outstanding stock of Aluminum Company of Canada Limited, and major interest in over thirty subsidiaries engaged in mining bauxite (aluminum ore); production and sale of aluminum; and production and sale of hydroelectric power.
Has reserves of raw material in British Guiana; smelting and fabricating plants in various parts of the world. All property in enemy territory written down in 1939-41. Capacity of Canadian plants steadily expanded since outbreak of war; capacity more than doubled in 1940, new $60,000,000 programme undertaken in 1941, and plans for further substantial increase put into effect early in 1942. Aluminum Power Company develops some 300,000 h.p. on Saguenay river; work currently under way on $35,000,000 project to bring in initial 500,000 h.p. at the Shipshaw site.
Then are set out the directors of Aluminium Limited, the parent company.
Is that a Canadian or a British firm ?

A Canadian firm. The directors are as follows:
E. K. Davis, President. Marston Mills, Mass.; E. Blough, E. G. MacDowell, G. O. Morgan, vice-presidents, Montreal; Hon. Leighton Mc-

Carthy, vice-president, Toronto; E. J. Mejia, vice-president, Geneva, Switzerland; T. H. Alger, vice-president, secretary and assistant treasurer; R. E. Powell, Aime Geoffrion, Montreal. Treasurer. J. F. Evans; assistant secretary, J. A. Dullea.
From this Survey of Corporate Securities of 1942 I checked the information which had come to me, and therefore I believe the statement I made on Friday was absolutely correct. Moreover this report gives Aluminium Limited as the parent company, and Aluminum Company of Canada Limited as the fully owned subsidiary of that concern together with Aluminum Power Company, Limited; Aluminum Union Limited; Northern Aluminum Company Limited; Aluminum Goods, Limited; Aluminium Laboratories Limited and Aluminium Securities Limited.
Consequently, I respectfully suggest that when I gave the information on Friday Mr. McCarthy was listed as director and vicepresident of this company in 1942. I go further and say that the statement issued by the Prime Minister-and it was a rather clever statement, which said that Mr. McCarthy had been replaced by Mr. Geoffrion as counsel in 1937 and was no longer a director -is true. I understand Mr. McCarthy resigned as director of Aluminum of Canada corporation in January of this year, and that seems to be confirmed by the report I have of corporate securities for 1942. And so I want to make a correction, because I was shocked to think that I had made the misstatement attributed to me. I find now that while I made a slip in calling it "Aluminum", which is my usual pronunciation of the word, I should have referred to the parent company, "Aluminium Limited". The error of pronunciation into which I fell I regret. Nevertheless I repeat the statement that according to this, the Survey of Corporate Securities for 1942, Mr. McCarthy is listed as a vice-president of the parent company of the Aluminum Company of Canada Limited, which is given here as Aluminium Limited.
Who publishes the Survey of Corporate Securities from which the hon. member reads?

The Maclean Publishing Company of Montreal, Toronto, New York and London, England. I think all hon. members will agree that members of the house regard this Survey of Corporate Securities, filed in the parliamentary library, as the standard work which we consult from time to time to get any authoritative information of this description we might require.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair there is a matter I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), namely, the cheese quota for 1943. Prior to the Easter adjournment, when the minister had received representations from various cheese producers throughout eastern Ontario and the western part of Quebec, I asked the minister if he would provide an opportunity for the discussion of the cheese quota and the price of cheese before the Easter adjournment. He replied that provision would be made for such discussion on his estimates. It was pointed out to the minister at that time that a discussion when the estimates were presented would be too late, because now is the time cheese factories have to get under way.
The urgency lies in the fact that the quota for the year is 150,000,000 pounds, and up to the present, with the first four months of 1943 gone, cheese production is down by at least 10,000,000 pounds over 1942. In 1942 slightly over 202.000,000 pounds were produced, representing an increase of 34-1 per cent over the 151,000,000 pounds produced in 1941.	_
The cheese producers of eastern Ontario, from whom the greater part of the quota will come, are asking the government to set the price of cheese only at a figure which will cover the increased cost of production in 1943 over that of 1942. The increase in price in 1943 over 1942 is five-eighths of a cent, whereas the increase in the cost of production, which will vary slightly in different districts, is from 3^ cents to slightly over 4i cents a pound. This increased cost of production is due to the increased cost of labour on the farm, increased cost of feeds, of maintenance, of delivery of milk from farms to factory, of labour in the factory, of factory supplies, of fuel, of cheese boxes and of trucking cheese from the factory to grading stations.
I should like to indicate how the increased cost over 1942 is arrived at. First, we will realize that the cost of labour has risen from about $45 a month to at least $60, working out at 2-4 cents per pound of cheese. The additional cost of feeds is placed at one cent a pound, whereas the increased manufacturing costs, including cheese boxes, fuel and other factory supplies stands at -2 cent. The increased cost of hauling milk to factory is [DOT][DOT]15 cent, making a total increase of 3'75 cents per pound of cheese.
The second example, produced from another factory shows an increased labour cost over 1942 of 2-24 cents a pound. The increase in the cost of feeds in this instance is placed at 1-24 cents a pound, and the maintenance cost is -20 cent. The increased cost of manufacturing is -19 cent, and that of trucking and hauling milk to factory is -4 cent, making a total increase of 4-27 cents per pound of cheese.
In 1942 the county of Hastings, in which I reside, produced nearly 12,000,000 pounds of cheese, a production greater than that of. any other county in Ontario. To-day in that county many cheese factories have not yet begun operations, one of the reasons being that more and more farmers are shipping cream, on account of the very satisfactory price, and the subsidy paid for that product. They are thereby able to retain their skimmed milk for calves and pigs. Owing also to the satisfactory price of fluid milk, more farmers are shipping fluid milk to the larger centres. Last year we had a very satisfactory and early spring, with ideal pasture and other conditions. The spring of 1943 is not as satisfactory in that respect. I should like to give a few quotations from various papers throughout the district. These articles give some indication of the decline in cheese production.
The Belleville Ontario Intelligencer of April 24 states that for the first quarter the cheese production in Hastings county is two-thirds less than it was in 1942. Giving the figures for one week only, the article points out that during the week ended April 24, only 899 cheese were produced as compared with 2,637 which were produced in the same week in 1942. The Ottawa Journal of May 10 of this year carried an editorial which was headed "Butter for Canada-or cheese for Britain?" The editorial points out that at a meeting of the cheese respresentatives of eastern Ontario, held in Toronto a few days previously, it was stated that there would be a serious reduction this year in the production of cheese and that it was doubtful whether Canada could fulfil her quota to Britain of 150,000,000 pounds. The editorial goes on to say:
The directors of the Ontario cheese producers' association made out a good case for patrons at the Toronto meeting. They left little doubt that patrons were dissatisfied with this year's set price, five-eighths of a cent above the 1942 price. Figures were produced to show that production costs had increased from three to four cents per pound of cheese.
The Toronto Globe and Mail of May 12-1 assume it is safe to refer to this publication- contains the following headlines:
Ontario Dairymen say 1943 cheese quota can't be filled; late seeding, low prices, are factors.

He believes the price of cheese should be twenty-two cents f.o.b. factory instead of twenty cents, and says farmers need the extra amount to cover higher costs of production.

He says, for example, the federal subsidy of two cents per quart retail on whole milk has whipped up the demand to such an extent that many farmers have switched from cheese to the more lucrative whole milk trade. The demand is so great that farmers are no longer plagued with surplus and hold-back milk.

The Toronto Globe and Mail of May 11 contains a dispatch from Kingston, Ontario, reading as follows:
The dairy products board, Ottawa, is insistent that cheese factories continue to operate regardless of the price which is being paid for milk delivered at the factories.
I should like to ask the minister if that is an indication of the compulsion which is to be practised by this production board. The cheese producers of Canada held a meeting at Peterborough on May 1, at which the following resolution was passed:
The executive of the Peterborough -county cheese producers'association is dissatisfied with the announced price for cheese, namely, twenty cents f.o.b. shipping points. This price will not meet the increase in cost of boxes and supplies compared with last year.
[DOT] '^'2? further, there is an increased cost and insufficient supply of farm labour.
It is definitely our opinion that the price will not secure maximum production required to meet the need of export and home markets. And further, this season is late and the figures to date prove that we are now considerably short in production compared with 1942. This is caused partly by the poor price received by cheese producers last winter, compared to 1942.
The monthly dairy report published by the Ontario department of agriculture refers to dairy production in the March issue, from which I quote as follows:
Cheese production shows a sharp reduction from the level a year ago. The February output for Ontario is reported at 1,090,000 pounds as against 2,633,800 pounds in February, 1942, a 
decrease of 41-4 per cent. For January and February the accumulated make is 2,504 500 pounds as compared with 5,712,800 pounds in the same period of last year, or a decline of 43-8 per cent.
I would. Tefer the Minister of Agriculture to an order in. council which was passed; on June 18, 1941, being P.C. 3696. This order in council states that the quota for 1941 was
112,000,000 pounds; that the. production, for the first four months in 1941 was 6,262,000 pounds less than the same period in 1940. It states also that the production of cheese in April showed a decrease of 1,222,000 pounds over the same month of 1940, and it goes on to say that in order to stimulate production the bonus of six-tenths of a cent per pound, which had been provided for by P.C. 143 in January, 1941, and which had not resulted in the increased production as anticipated, and as ninety-three, per cent, of the. cheese produced in Canada and practically all the cheese exported is produced in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, would be increased to one and six-tenths cents per pound.
When the order in council was passed the minister pointed out- that the production of cheese was down by 6,262,000 pounds for the first four months, whereas to-day production is down by at least 10,000,000 pounds. In 1941 the quota for Great Britain was
112,000,000 pounds, whereas the quota this year is 150,000,000 pounds. If the minister felt then that it was necessary to increase the subsidy or the bonus in order to get the amount required for the quota, surely the same condition applies, and' doubly so, during the present year.
There is one further matter I should like to bring to the attention of the minister, a matter which was brought up by the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser). Because of a shortage of labour many cheese factories are discontinuing the manufacture of whey butter, and the ration board has ruled that a farmer must deliver butter coupons in order to purchase this product. It naturally follows that if these factories discontinue making whey butter there will be less cream sent to the creameries and less milk sent to the cheese factories, because the average farmer will keep his milk and cream at home and manufacture his own butter. I suggest to the minister that he review the whole question of whey butter and see if something cannot be done whereby the farmer may purchase whey butter without having to give up butter coupons.
The need of .the farmer receiving a better price for his produce has been stated time and again in this house. Everyone knows that the farmer is making a supreme effort at the

present time, and if he is expected to increase his cheese production this year to fill the quota, he is certainly entitled to a price which will ensure him the same.return as he received last year. Therefore I ask the minister to give serious attention to these considerations and to review the various briefs, letters and telegrams which have been submitted to him by various cheese associations in eastern Ontario. Then I trust he will see fit to make a proper adjustment in the price of cheese so that the-farmer will receive in 1943 at least the same return as he had in 1942.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot help rising to say a few words along the same line as that taken by the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White). A little while ago I attended a meeting of the war committee on agricultural production in my riding and was greatly concerned over their anxiety as to the production of cheese in the coming year in Carleton county and the surrounding community. As we all know, the season is late, and that has reacted seriously on the production of cheese. Some of the factories there are not yet open for production, and many of them are running at very low capacity, not producing anything like the amount of cheese they did last year. There is also the shortage of help, reduction of herds and other factors which, while perhaps not directly affecting cheese more than other products, have reduced the supply of milk to the factories, so that a definite drop in production is taking place.
Not long ago I attended a meeting of the cheese producers' association in my community which considered the price of cheese, and there was great discontent as to the price for the coming year as compared with last year. According to their calculation, the increase amounts to but five-eighths of a cent a pound in that community. I asked several representative factories in my community to give me figures as to the increased costs of production of cheese. These percentages are taken from individual factories and are to a very slight degree estimates and to a very great degree actual figures, which I should like to place before the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) for his consideration.
First of all, there has been a great increase in wages paid for farm help. Not only is the farm help situation critical so far as the supply of man-power is concerned, but it is demanding a much higher rate of wages. The increase in the wages of farm help is estimated at thirty per cent over the wages of last year. The price of milk cows in my community is probably thirty-five per cent higher than it was last year, and the cost of
feed is 15 per cent higher. Cheese boxes have actually increased in price 14-3 per cent over that of last year. Cheese makers' wages, the labour content in the production of cheese, have increased substantially, by 16-1 per cent, and fuel costs have increased by 14-3 per cent over those of last year. All these increased costs of production amount to between three and four cents per pound of cheese. The increased price to the producer this year represents five-eighths of one cent, which is not nearly enough to compensate him for the increased costs which he has to meet.
Statistics which have already been put on Hansard by the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough show the material reduction that has taken place in the production of cheese this year. We are now in the middle of May, and in ordinary years one could tell pretty accurately at this time of the year what the cheese production for the coming year would be. I sincerely believe that if we are to fill our quota of cheese for export in the coming year, something must be done at once. So far as my own community is concerned, I believe that there will be a substantial decrease in the cheese production this year. The production of whole milk and cream is much more profitable for the farmer. With the many difficulties which the cheese producers are experiencing in Carleton, Lanark, Grenville, Peterborough and many counties of eastern Ontario which are substantial cheese producers and contribute materially to the quota for the export market, I think the present situation should receive the urgent attention and further consideration of the Department of Agriculture at Ottawa. It is true that the provincial government raised the price of cheese last year and again this year, but that does not compensate the producer for the increased costs of production. May I in all kindness, yet with great anxiety, ask the Minister of Agriculture to reconsider the whole cheese situation? I believe that he has already received delegations from the producers of cheese in Ontario, and I would not be doing my duty if I did not emphasize the urgency of immediate action in the present situation.

Mr. Speaker, before the Minister of Agriculture replies, I wish to say a word on butter, and perhaps he can deal with the two subjects at the same time.
Some months ago a ration was placed on butter in Canada on the theory that there were shortages and scarcity in certain places. With that I have no great fault to find. There was a spotty condition and there were shortages. At the same time there were other places where there were surpluses.
Cheese Quota-Whey Butter

To-day, from the information I have received, there is no longer any scarcity of butter in Canada. We are now in the process of accumulating a surplus sufficiently large to carry us over the next short season. In the interim the policy was adopted, under the aegis of the wartime prices and trade board, I believe, of shipping butter into what were called deficiency areas. That I think was probably a fair and good practice at the time, 'but it had some very strange results. The maritime provinces, including New Brunswick, with regard to which I have some slight knowledge of the situation, was declared to be a deficiency area. New Brunswick was, with respect to creameiy butter, deficient, but it was not a deficiency area having regard to the fact that 60 per cent of the entire butter production of the province is dairy processed butter. The rationing process had the effect of preventing in a very large measure the marketing of the dairy processed butter. The policy of rushing supplies into deficiency areas took away from some of the creamery companies in that province a market for their surplus production. For instance, Cape Breton was a deficiency area. The production there I assume is small, and importations have to be made twelve months in the year from other parts of Canada. One of the largest butter factories in New Brunswick had been in the habit of finding a ready market year in and year out in the Sydney area of Cape Breton. But as a result of the action of the authorities, the wartime prices and trade board, I presume, the Sydney area was filled from outside the maritime provinces, with the result that the creamery companies which looked upon it as their natural outlet for their surplus have to-day no market at all for their surplus production and are accumulating surpluses which they are finding it difficult to store. No matter how good was the intention of the board-and I am not going to question their bona fides-the situation which now presents itself shows the danger of interfering with the orderly marketing of consumer goods, such as butter, which are so necessary in this country. I am dealing with the matter in only its local aspects, and with no relation to our production of milk products for overseas or the army. But I am drawing attention to a situation which now exists.
Furthermore, I had a letter from the executive of another creamery company stating that as a result of the action of the board he was unable to market his surplus and unable to find proper storage for it, and he did not know what he was going to do with it.
There has grown up, even in the winter months, a substantial surplus of dairy processed butter, notwithstanding the remedial measures 
which were attempted under the policy of the board. That had a bad effect. I know of a man in Carleton county who had sixty milch cows, some of them in production, and he had to dry them up because he could not sell his production.
These people were told in the winter months, "Send your cream to the creameries." It seemed as though the whole policy of the board was to drive the milk producers into patronizing the creameries. I remember voicing this complaint once before in this house, and the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Leclerc), I think it was, interjected, "Why don't you sell your milk to the creameries?" That was not possible during a winter like last winter. The provincial government of New Brunswick refused to plough any but the main trunk roads. Furthermore, there was a scarcity of gasoline and truckage so far as the major creamery companies were concerned. Whatever one's opinion may be about the quality of the production as between the creameries and farmer processed butter, let me tell the minister that in New Brunswick sixty per cent is dairy processed and sixty per cent of the people prefer it, on the theory that if you know the man who makes it, it is better butter. I myself believe in the theory that the farmer processed butter is on the whole better butter than the creamery butter. But I realize that the modern trend is to manufacture creamery butter, because in the large markets like Montreal it is the only kind which is marketable. There will have to be a process of education in the country before the people come to that conclusion.
In the meantime what has happened is this. A very large bonus has been given to the producers of creamery butter. A farmer came into my office during the Easter vacation and told me what he was getting, and of course it was most satisfactory to him ; he was shipping his production to a creamery. Another farmer who came to see me was not in that happy position, and he was not getting the same sort of treatment from the federal treasury that the first farmer was. An attempt was made, and I think it was probably the best thing that could be done at the time, to instruct retail and wholesale merchants to buy this farmer processed butter; yet the rationing process has prevented the rapid consumption and distribution among the consumers of this type of butter. As a consequence there is a real grievance in New Brunswick. I do not know how things may be elsewhere. The butter policy of the country to-day is anathema to sixty per cent of the producers, and more than sixty per cent hold the opinion, whether rightly or wrongly'-rightly, I think-that they

Cheese Quota-Whey Butter
are being discriminated against by the policy of the government in this matter of bonusing butter. I believe that a substantial surplus has already accumulated. A figure has been stated in the press; I do not know that it is authoritative. The minister, undoubtedly, knows what the surplus in storage to-day is.
I am wondering whether the whole position should not be reviewed, at least in so far as certain areas are concerned. It is not my purpose to impute motives to those who established this policy. No doubt their motives were good, but. the operation of the policy and- the regulations established under it have pressed very hardly on some of our people.
I have found that that is true with respect to other policies of the wartime prices and trade board. Recently it was stated that there was a shortage of potatoes in this country. I have seen, not the order in council, but the regulations which were promulgated by the wartime prices and trade board through their director at Toronto. I tell the house that those regulations were entirely in the interests of the distribution trade and ignored entirely the trade which had to do with the collection and sale of potatoes to the distributors in the big centres. Certainly the producer was altogether ignored.
Let me give the minister an illustration of how this thing works. Every contract was frozen. Every commitment for the sale of potatoes was cancelled. Every shipment, unless the potatoes were in cars, rolling, was frozen. Shippers were instructed that they should no longer consign cars to individual purchasers but that they should be consigned through their banks, not to an individual but for the account of the wartime prices and trade board and subject to directions from them. No doubt that method of control was deemed necessary by those in authority. But the thing went a good deal further. Dealers in large centres like Montreal, who were aware that for a short period before the new crop was in, further supplies would be required, and who were diligent and businesslike, and made purchases, and had cars actually on track at the point of delivery, found themselves confronted with an order taking away these shipments from them and handing them over to their competitors who had not any foresight or forethought. I have it on the authority of the hon. member for Yictoria-Carleton (Mr. Hatfield) that in one case five carloads of New Brunswick potatoes on track at Montreal, purchased by a man who had the foresight to provide for his customers and patrons, were diverted to a competitor who had not bought a single carload. Such a proceeding is anything but desirable.
I think that was a gross discrimination against this dealer who was provident and in favour of his competitor who was improvident. That sort of thing cannot be justified on any ground. I am quite aware that the minister is in no sense responsible, and I am not suggesting .that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley), under whose aegis the wartime prices and trade board operates, is responsible. But it goes to show how arbitrary these boards are sometimes. The illustration I have given is really the limit, when you take five carloads of produce laid down in one big centre, one big market, and hand them over to a competitor to sell to his customers in the same market. I do not think I need do more than state that fact, if it is a fact-and I have given the source of my information. That sort of thing is most arbitrary and causes the greatest discontent, and because the hon. member who gave me-the information, has been ill I took it upon, myself to communicate with the authorities direct. I made it clear to them that I was not quarrelling with the underlying principle of control, but what I was complaining about was the operation under the regulations, and I have tried to make the point here to-day.
I think something has to be done about the butter situation. The dairy producers to-day are labouring undier a discrimination of at least eight cents a pound, and they are subject to the rationing of the commodity at Fredericton, where hundreds of pounds a,re n^arketed every Wednesday and Saturday. They must sell on a ration basis, and the farmers bring in their boxes of butter and simply take them away because people have not the ration coupons to give them. There is the greatest dissatisfaction because they cannot dispose of their butter as freely as heretofore-and butter is abundantly available. And, in addition, they have to take a lower price.
I beg the minister and those in authority to review the whole position in the light of the great production that is now upon us in butter. The farmers in our country are now producing butter, not cheese. It is much more favourable to sell milk for butter or to produce butter at home than it is to send the milk to the cheese factories. I will not go into the merits or demerits of the discrepancy between the price for butter and the price for cheese. I leave that to someone more competent than I. There is, however, a discrepancy. A while ago it was the other way, and it was more profitable to produce cheese than butter, but to-day the reverse is the
