position. Men are getting the equivalent of fifty-three cents for milk for butter, and it is much less than that for cheese.
Butter fat?

Yes, with the bonus and everything. My hon. friend is Minister of Agriculture,, and I make a direct appeal to him on behalf of the farmers and the dairy producers in my county who have written letters of protest in the newspapers and who have written to me time and again protesting against the inequality under which they contend they are suffering and will continue to suffer until the position is altered in some way. You cannot tell these people they should not make their own butter. This is a free country and they resent the restrictions which are put upon them, and certainly resent the discrimination in price.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
speechtext:
With regard to the remarks made by the last speaker (Mr. Hanson), I have only a very few statements to make. The first is that the wartime prices and trade board, as has been explained to this house on a number of occasions, have been attempting to regulate prices and, in so far as these particular commodities are concerned, to regulate food prices as part of the policy under which they have been attempting to avoid inflation in Canada. All of those who have spoken with regard to the matter from time to time, whether to-day or previously, have admitted that it is necessary that a policy with that objective in mind should be enforced in Canada. As has been suggested by the last speaker, the Department of Agriculture should keep, and it has been keeping, as close a check as possible upon the results of the operation of any of the controls that may be imposed on food, and I must say the prices board have been keeping in very close touch with the officials of the department from time to time, while the officials of the department have also been in very close touch with the board. There are times when discussions are necessary in order to arrive at final conclusions as to what ought to be done.
I am not in a position this afternoon to state exactly what the situation is in regard to the supply of potatoes. I had no information before coming into the house that this discussion would take place. But at the earliest possible date I shall have full information and be in a position to deal with the matter. I only wish to state at the moment that shortages in connection with the supply of potatoes-at certain points have developed, and some inconvenience has arisen in consequence. Those shortages have taken place

largely in city centres where it is rather difficult to obtain any emergency supplies which may be available on certain farms throughout the country. It is impossible for one without notice to deal with individual cases such as that which is stated to have developed in Montreal, but the facts with regard to those cases can be found and' placed before the house in due course. I shall see that full inquiry is made into the matter, and any announcements that can be made, as a result of experience gained, can be made at a later time, and as soon as possible.
With regard to the butter situation, I agree with the hon. gentleman when he says that there are increased supplies of butter. The butter stocks on May 1, 1943, amounted to
10.022.000	pounds, and on May 1, 1942, to
5.878.000	pounds.
Are those figures based on warehouse receipts?

Stock in store in warehouses across Canada on May 1. The butter stocks for 1941 were 9,630,000 pounds. When one takes these three years, not only the last two years, and- makes comparisons it will be seen that in 1943 as compared with 1941 there is little difference. The storage as at the first of May, 1941, was 9,630,000 pounds, and in 1943 at the first of May it is 10,022,000 pounds. There is not sufficient difference for us to be concerned about the amount available when one takes into consideration that the consumption of butter is very much greater now than it was two years ago.
Mr. 8ENN: What is considered a normal supply of butter?
The figure for 1941 is not very far from normal.
I was under the impression that it was higher than that.

I do not think it would be lower than that, in any event, which would mean that the amount of 10,022,000 pounds is nothing on which to base a conclusion that we ought to be doing something about an overproduction of butter at this stage.
Has the minister the figures in regard to the increase in the production, of butter in 1941 and 1942, or the increase this year as compared with last year?

The production of
creamery butter for the first three .months of 1943 was 40.599,000 pounds; for the first three months of last year, 31,777,000 pounds; and for the year before that, 34,126,000 pounds.

Cheese Quota-Whey Butter
To give it for the complete years, in 1942 the production was 284,000,000 pounds; in 1941, 285,000,000 pounds; in 1940, 264,000,000 pounds, and in 1939, 267,000,000 pounds, all in round figures. So that the production last year was approximately the same as in the preceding year and 20,000,000 pounds more than the year before, but it is estimated that this year the production wdll be considerably higher than last year. Therefore, when one takes the production figures, the storage figures and

if we had them at the moment, which I have not-the consumption figures, it would be found that there is no considerable difference this year as compared with some preceding years.
I think what the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) had in mind principally was the question of dairy butter. I have not the facts in that regard up to date, but I have them for the period under review when we last discussed this matter in the house. Before the Easter recess certain hon. members called attention to the condition which existed because butter had been rationed, and stated that dairy butter was left upon a market in which there was very little demand. At that time the wartime prices and trade board made provision whereby the corporation set up under that board would take delivery of butter. Speaking from memory^ I believe the result was that well under a thousand pounds of butter were located in the city of Saint John during the weeks immediately following that discussion in the house. The last time I checked the figures they indicated that this amount of butter had been obtained in the city of Saint John, and that this accounted for -most of the butter which had been obtained in New Brunswick, while something in the neighbourhood of seven thousand pounds had been obtained across Canada in the same period of time. I have had the officials of the department keeping a check on that situation since then. They are under instructions to report any time serious difficulties might develop in connection with the dairy butter offered for sale across the country. In recent weeks no reports have been made to me, but the question having been raised again I shall examine into the circumstances now existing and report as soon as possible upon the present situation in various parts of Canada in relation to dairy butter.
The discussion taking place at the moment , arose as a result of statements made by the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White) with regard to cheese, and for a moment I should like to deal with that situa-. tion. Stocks of cheese as at May 1, 1943,
amounted to 17,212,000 pounds. On May 1, 1942, our stocks of cheese totalled 29,039,000 pounds, while on May 1, 1941, they were
15,609,000	pounds, or about 1,600,000 pounds less than this year. I recite the figures for these three years in order to point out that the facts-and they are facts-which were placed upon the record a few moments ago by the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough, and concurred in by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Boucher), do not necessarily place one in a position to arrive at a sound conclusion. There are special reasons why the production of cheese was very high in the spring of 1942. One was the fact that the wartime prices and trade board, on the advice of the Department of Agriculture and at the request of cheese producers, fixed a price of twenty-five cents for cheese during the winter months of 1941-42. That was done because during the summer of 1941 we had taken off the Canadian market all the cheese produced in Ontario and Quebec, and sent it to Britain. We did not allow any of the production of that season to remain on the market, but sent it to Britain in order to meet the contract of that year. We asked the Canadian people to go without cheese during that summer, and they did so. Then the following winter we asked the farmers to produce cheese as they had never produced it before. They did so, and we paid them an unusually high price for that cheese in order to get it during the winter of 1941-42, to supply the Canadian market with a product that would not be acceptable to the British market. As every hon. member knows, the best Canadian cheese is produced in the summer months, when the cattle are on the grass, and it is that cheese we desired to have to send to the British market. This winter-produced cheese was intended for and, I think, largely marketed in Canada. That is one reason why it is not altogether useful to compare production during the first four or five months of 1942 with production during the first four months of 1943, because we are working under entirely different conditions. . When we compare the stocks on hand on May 1, 1943, with the stocks on hand on May 1, 1941, and find that in 1943 we have more than we had in 1941, then I think we are making a useful comparison in connection with this question.
There are other reasons why our production would be down this year as compared with last year. As every hon. member knows, and as we realize when we look at the weather, this season is at least four weeks later than last season. Our production of dairy products this year is not up to the mark of last year because
Cheese Quota-Whey Butter

then we had an early season and this year we have a late season. Perhaps if one took an average as between the two he would not be far wide of the mark as to what should be an average condition. Then, too, all through 1942 dairy farmers and their representatives were telling the wartime prices and trade board and the Department of Agriculture, and through those bodies the government, that the returns for cheese were comparatively high, and as a result we were getting cheese at the expense of butter and at the expense of canned and whole milk.
At what point of time would that be?

I would say that all
through the summer of 1942 representations were made to that effect. During the winter of 1942-43, about the time the Department of Agriculture took over the control of subsidies for production, we were asked to pay a subsidy of twenty-five cents a hundred on milk that was to be processed. We placed that subsidy on, and made it retroactive over the month of March, so that it covered March and April. That subsidy was taken off on May 1. Many of the representations made to the government and to the press were made during April, when there was a subsidy of twenty-five cents a hundred on milk, to keep it in processing plants-and which did keep it in processing plants, at the expense of cheese factories. So that the production of cheese during the last weeks of April would, of necessity, be lower than in seasons when conditions of that kind did not prevail, in connection with subsidies.
Someone asked a moment ago whether certain statements which had been or which, according to newspaper reports, were presumed to have been made, might be considered in the nature of an intention to enforce some kind of compulsion. I would say, no; they do not necessarily mean that at all. But they do mean that if certain practices which have been carried on by certain people in certain limited areas are to continue until next fall, the government may have to reconsider the question of paying subsidies on milk for certain purposes.
What are the practices?
Practices of the kind where persons would go into certain areas and induce others to take milk away from cheese factories, because the subsidy for other purposes has increased the price of milk.
It would be a diversion.

Yes; it would be diverted from a district which usually made cheese into one having some other activity.
There may be no necessity to inflict compulsion, but it may be necessary to reconsider the subsidies being paid. I repeat that the representations made all through last year, and right down until the announcement made in the house within the last few weeks respecting the policy for this summer, were to the effect that the returns for cheese were higher than the returns for milk for other purposes. Based upon that representation, the subsidies were increased or retained on whole milk, and were increased for summer production of butter. They had previously been increased for winter production of butter. I make this statement only in order to have the facts on the record.
Has the dairy products board power at its discretion to order farmers to send their milk either to a cheese factory, to some other processing factory, or to a butter factory?
I should not like to say they have the power. I have grave doubts as a matter of fact as to whether they have.
But they have done it.

But I would say that cheese factories, butter factories and processing plants have all cooperated with the dairy board, when they have been asked to do so. And when, in connection with the production of food, representations have been made to the effect that it would be more in the interests of Britain or of Canada, or more in the interests of the dairy industry itself to do certain things, they have cooperated to the greatest possible extent, in order to bring about the desired result. I do not think any compulsion will be necessary in order to get the results desired both by the dairy people and by the board.
I asked the question because I have seen reports in the newspapers which would indicate compulsion.

I saw that report, too. I can assure the hon. member no compulsion was used in the matter. Any changes which have been made have taken place as a result of discussions among parties concerned. There has been one case where they had to go back and have a second discussion, but I think it will be found in the end that all parties will cooperate, and see that the proper thing is done.

One will see therefore, from checking these records, that there were only four years since 1914, and those were toward the end of and immediately succeeding the last war, when cheese was as high as it was in 1942. And it is higher than that in 1943. One must remember, -too, that while in 1942 the price of cheese was 21-5 cents, there was in addition to that a premium added by this government, and a subsidy of two cents a pound by each of the governments of Ontario and Quebec. The premium was as high as two cents a pound, with the result that the average price ipaid for cheese, plus the subsidies, ini 1942 was around twenty-four cents a pound. For this year the average return will be over twenty-five cents, with payments made on the same basis as last year.
So that if one takes those facts into consideration he will find there were only two years, namely 1919 and 1920, when cheese brought a higher return than it did in 1942, or higher than it will bring in 1943. I think this should be said in order to keep hon. members fully informed as to the price being paid to-day, in relation to prices paid at other times.

So that in 1943 we are obtaining a price more than double the price obtained in 1939, the year immediately preceding the war.
I place these figures on record in order to show what I have already said to the cheese producers, when they have been here, namely, that it is hardly fair to compare 1942 with 1943, and then say we should have an increase in price in 1943 over 1942, to take care of all increases in cost of production, as between those two years.
Is it not a fact that the quota for overseas is larger than it was in 1942?

I shall deal with that later. Cheese increased in price from five-eighths of a cent to a cent a pound. The average increase is not five-eighths of a cent. There is an additional amount equal to the freight when shipping from points removed from Montreal into that city. This produces an increase from five-eighths of a cent to one cent, and the increase brings the price of cheese under the British contract up close to twenty-one cents at Montreal.
As I was stating, it is hardly fair to take all the increase in the cost of production which has occurred this year and charge it all up to the fact that there has not been a great enough increase in the price as between 1941 and- 1942. That statement is borne out by these figures. The average price of cheese in April, 1941, was 14-9 cents a pound; the average price in April, 1942, was 21-2 cents a pound, an increase of 6-2 cents. If one takes the whole year he will find that the price established with Great Britain in 1941 was 15 cents a pound, whereas the price established in the succeeding year was 20 cents, a difference of 5 cents a pound. That increase last year of 5 cents a pound was placed for the purpose of obtaining a greater production of 1942 than had ever been obtained before. The government deliberately paid more for cheese than it had ever paid before; the government deliberately put cheese out of line with every other dairy product in order to get a higher production in
1942	than we had ever had before since the beginning of the century. The desired results were obtained, and in 1942 we got a cheese production of 202,000,000 pounds. When we are not asking for an increased production in
1943	it would seem fair to take care of the increased cost by making allowance for this fact.

I have stated to the house before, and I am going to state it more plainly now, that in the fall of 1942 we were asked by the British government to consider the necessity of delivering less cheese to Britain in 1942 because she had made arrangements elsewhere which seemed to fill her demands. As a result of that request, we opened the boundary line into the United States and sold several million pounds of cheese in that country in order to take off the market some of what otherwise would have been a surplus. Just following that experience, we arranged for the conference in Decerriber which was held to talk over the production of different farm products. At that time it was represented that we should ask for a decrease in the production of cheese in Canada; not an increase, but a decrease. Knowing that situations change very rapidly in war time, I warned against asking for a decrease in cheese production and suggested that we should maintain it at the same level, in so far as our request was concerned. A little later on we received representations from Britain to the effect that she had been rather disappointed in her supplies last year from outside Canada ' and would appreciate it very much if we would try this year to give her 150,000,000 pounds of cheese-
At the time that request came through, our storages of cheese in Canada were unusually high and it was not necessary to call for production in order to obtain the supplies which were to go to Britain earlier in this season. There were storages in existence which made possible some shipments to Britain in the early part of this season. As soon as that request was received, we suggested to the farmers that we would like them to keep their production up to a point where we could supply 150,000,000 pounds of cheese to Britain this year. I wish to state that it is not necessary to produce
202,000,000 pounds of cheese in order to supply Britain with 150,000,000 pounds of cheese this year. In other words, the fact that there may be some decrease in the production of cheese will not necessarily endanger the cheese contract we have with Great Britain. There are other means by which the situation could be met if it were found that production was going to go down to an extent which would seriously endanger the contract we have with Great Britain.
Having said that, I come back to the point which was raised by the first speaker, the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough, who made a comparison between the production of last year and the production of this year. My advices are that we have not yet reached the point where we can be sure that we shall not be able to produce all the cheese

in Canada, even under the situation as it now exists, which it will be necessary to produce in order to fill the contract which we have with Britain for 1943. If the time comes when we find or we believe that nothing more is necessary than what has been done up to date, the announcement will be made, but I think members of the house will agree that until we have more conclusive evidence a change is necessary, the policy which ought to be followed is the one announced.
When will that time be?

It may be within the next few weeks. As I said a few moments ago, we are about four weeks late. We had experiences at this time last year with regard to the production of cheese which indicated to us that there was no doubt we would get more cheese than we had asked for and less butter than we needed!.

The indications now are the
reverse.

At the present time the indications are that we may get more butter than we need. However, there is nothing conclusive about that, as the figures I gave a few moments ago will indicate. We may get more butter than we need, but we must remember that there is always a place to put it. I hesitate at this moment to say that the facts indicate that it is necessary for us to make any change in the policy which was announced. I should like to call the attention of the house and the country to the fact that we were asked, and asked' continuously, to announce a polics' this year which would cover the whole line of dairy products throughout the year. We have officials who are considered to be more or less expert in this matter. They sat down, along with others, and worked out the prices which were to be established for the different products and the subsidies which, were to be paid in relation to the prices in order to bring them to a common level.
I regret to say that immediately we had that worked out we were asked to increase the price of cheese. Last year the price of cheese *was higher than the prices of other products, and we were asked to bring the other prices up to that of cheese. I am informed that we have not yet passed the price of cheese with the prices of most if not all of the other dairy products, but they have been brought up somewhere in the neighbourhood of the price of cheese. It is my opinion that we ought to let the plan operate sufficiently long to be able to determine what

the results will be before we go to the treasury to ask them to put up more money in order to place the price of cheese out of line with prices of other commodities. We would then probably have to come along later and say that we must bring the other prices up to the new level of cheese.
So far, we believe that the plan has functioned fairly well. Before sitting down, I must say that the representatives of the dairy people who came to us asked for a cent to a cent and a half or maybe close to two cents more than we are now paying for cheese. We did not consider it wise, after having taken all the facts and circumstances into consideration in our calculations, to meet that request. There are some substitutions which may have to be made for activities which have taken place in other places during recent weeks in order to arrive at the position we expected to reach when we had these discussions, but I am hopeful that the position will be reached. I am hopeful that the dairy industry will continue this year to produce what we require to meet the contracts we have made and to feed our people as well.

GOAL-PROCLAMATION DECLARING EXISTENCE OF A STATE OF EMERGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hesitate at this time to take up any time of the house, and I shall be as brief and explicit as possible. Members of this group have agreed that the question now before the house should be disposed of as expeditiously as possible. In view, however, of the announcement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) this afternoon of the authorization of the issue of a proclamation declaring a national fuel emergency in Canada, I am compelled to make a few remarks.
The Prime Minister stated this afternoon that he would welcome suggestions from members with respect to the fuel situation in Canada, in regard to which an order in council is to be passed shortly. Coming from a constituency where considerable coal mining is carried on, I have on many occasions discussed in the house the fuel situation and the developing crisis and tried to point out exactly where we were heading. Unfortunately, as a parliament we have neglected to do many things which we should have done with respect to the fuel situation, and as a result we are faced with an emergency to-day.
The thing I am concerned about-not merely interested in but concerned about- is the fact that an order in council is to be passed making it compulsory for men to be taken out of other industries and sent back to work in the coal mining industry'. I see no solution in that particular line unless it is very carefully worked out by men who are not only familiar with marketing requirements but actually know something about the production of coal and are prepared to handle the whole matter in the best interests of all concerned.
The newspapers this afternoon state that an order in council is to be passed and that certain things are to be done respecting the
Coal Emergency

coal mining industry. I understand that one of the proposals is the use of women on the surface of the mines. That is something new in Canada, and it will have to be very carefully handled. In the coal mining areas of Canada there are many men and boys available who could do any work around the surface of the mines essential to the handling of coal and the handling of materials that are necessary in the production of coal. I would emphasize that before any attempt is made to employ women around the surface of coal mines, every available man in the area should first be used. It has been intimated to me that the order in council which is to be passed will permit girls sixteen years of age to take work on and around the surface of a coal mine. I object to that. I think there is no necessity for it at this time. I believe that in every section of Canada where fuel is produced suitable male labour can be found to take care of the surface requirements.
Second, there is this to be considered. Men have left the coal mining industry and gone into other industries, the shipbuilding industry, for instance. Shipbuilding is, in my opinion, the first consideration of Canada to-day. If any attempt is made to take the men who have left the coal mining industry for other industries and transfer them back to the coal mining industry without some regard being paid to the wages they are now earning in specialist occupations for which they have been trained in the field of shipbuilding, it will be a mistake. Every man who has left the coal mines for some other industry has left the coal mines to better his condition. I have said before, that going to war is a vacation to some of the miners of Nova Scotia who work underground producing coal. You cannot just pass an order in council and then take away from the shipbuilding industry, we will say, a man who has been earning there from seventy to eighty cents an hour and send him back to work underground in the coal mines at a great reduction in wages, in a back-breaking and 100 per cent more hazardous occupation. Some regard will have to be had to the cooperation of the man himself, if he is to produce the coal. I think it would be a mistake to go into a shipyard where there are perhaps two or three or four hundred men who have left the coal mines and are now working in the shipyard as specialists and force them to go back to the coal mines to work at lower wages. This particular angle will have to be worked out very carefully with the representatives of the miners' unions, and I hope that is being done.
There are many mines in Nova Scotia where production cannot be increased over any long period of time. Many of the mines are old, and the programme for the last ten years has been in the direction of conserving their resources and reallocating the collieries. Some collieries have been closed down since the outbreak of war. That production cannot be replaced. You may crowd a lot of men into a coal mine and get increased production for a short period, but that is bad mining practice which will cripple the industry in the future. If it is increased production we want, we should have gone into that field three years ago to expand the industry. We have already suggested that in the house. It would be not only a war-time project; it is necessary as a post-war project also. That is something to which consideration should be given when we are dealing with the fuel situation as an emergency one.
There are many other angles which I should like to discuss, but I do not want to delay the house. I rose at this time for the purpose of urging those who are to draft the order in council to keep close to the men who are to be affected by it and to give careful consideration to the proposal of transferring men from war industries where they are doing specialists' jobs for which they have been trained, particularly in shipbuilding, and sending them back to the coal mines to work, unless regard is paid to the higher wages they are now receiving. The men could be appealed to on the basis of patriotism and in the interests of Canada's war effort, but certainly they should not just be compelled to go back to something which they left to better their condition, because you cannot live very long doing the job they have been doing in the coal mines of Nova Scotia for the past ten years. These collieries are old and on the wane, and a programme of expansion is necessary in Nova Scotia.
Now that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) is in his seat, I should like to bring this matter to his attention. During the past six months I have received many letters from men in the armed forces in Canada who were desirous of returning to the coal mines, as proposed by the department, for a three-month period in order to take employment there. Something was wrong with the machinery, because I have had at least fifty letters during this session from different parts of Canada from men who made application to their commanding officers requesting permission to take advantage of this offer, and in no case was action taken.

After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Before recess I was directing the attention of the committee to the necessity for a very careful scrutiny and examination of all expenditures. Particularly during war time is this necessary, when people are asked and are willing to make sacrifices to the end that victory shall be ours. My reason for addressing these few remarks to the committee is to call its attention and that of the minister to the necessity for an even closer scrutiny of expenditures than we have had heretofore, because I believe that the Canadian people expect us to do an all-out job to prevent waste and overexpenditure as far as possible. In my opinion, the greatest check on waste and extravagance is the giving of publicity to examples of either.
Now that the victory loan campaign has been such a success, and all of us in this house have contributed toward making it that success, and the people having discharged their responsibilities, I submit that we on our part must to a greater extent accept responsibility for a close scrutiny and examination of expenditures. Recently mention was made of the very high salaries paid to certain officials in the war information board, and by reason of the publicity given in this house changes have taken place which have resulted in savings. I am sure that further savings will take place.
Let me refer to one case and ask the Minister of Transport to answer the question as to what is being done with reference to this matter. I refer to the case of Doctor Chartier, of Montreal, a well-known medical man who, in part, looks after the medical administration of the Government Employees' Compensation Act. I asked the question on April 14, in regard to Doctor Chartier, a'nd the answer which was given at that time was that in a period of less than three years, or approximately three years, he had received in medical fees the sum of around $90,000. I did not get the information, nor could I have got the information regarding this case from an examination of either the auditor general's report or the estimates. The estimates for 1913-44, at page 222, indicate that the cost of administration of the act by the minister's department in the year 1943-44 will amount to $24,735, and that in 1942-43 it amounted to $23,322. Certainly neither of these estimates contains the item with reference to this doctor.
Before recess the Minister of Finance suggested that full information could be obtained from these reports. At page 424 of the auditor

general's report the total expenditure in the administration of the Government Employees' Compensation Act was given at only $20,625.91, and a casual examination of this particular report would indicate that that was all that the administration cost. Then on page 425 we find that, the total expenditure, for compensation, medical aid and administration, amounted to $489,297.40. Perhaps I should preface what I have to say by reading section 49 of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, namely, chapter 27 of the acts of 1931. If hon. gentlemen read the preceding sections they will see specific and meticulous directions under part 5 of this statute relating to the auditor general and his office. Section 39 provides for his appointment and his salary. It provides that he shall be appointed by the governor in council under the great seal. He is a very important official. Section 40 provides for his tenure of office during good behaviour and indicates that he is removable by the governor general on address by parliament. There is an age limit of seventy years, and so on. I desire to call attention to succeeding sections of the statute which set out his duties. The only one I am going to read is section 49:
The auditor general shall report annually to the House of Commons the result of his examination and audit of the accounts of Canada-
Mark these words, please:
-in such manner as will exhibit the true state of each account at the termination of the fiscal year last ended.
That is a specific direction to the auditor general, and I ask hon. members who have been following these reports in years gone by if they will just go back in their memory and compare the accounting system that we had until a year or two ago witn the present system. I will say this, that-due, I imagine, to the stress of the volume of work; probably that is a fair thing to say- the auditor general has departed almost entirely from that which by the custom and

Interim Supply Bill
sanction of decades the people of Canada have expected from him. To-day you do not know where the money goes. I venture to say that no one can take this report to-day and find out where the money has gone, as you could in the old days.

Where does your own
money go?

I think I could give a pretty fair answer to that if I went over my cheque book, though I could not say as much for the petty cash. In these days of high taxation I, like everyone else in this country, have to watch the dollars even if I do not watch the pence. I say that to-day the auditor general's report is not in conformity either with custom or with the instructions of parliament, and the position should be reversed.
I want now to go back to the original reference I gave to the committee, the statement signed by the auditor general and included under the heading of "general observations" and the specific heading of "revenue and expenditure reporting." I am going to ask hon. members to read these paragraphs, which cover three or four pages. There is too much for me to read in this chamber now and put on the record; hon. members could not. digest it as I went along. A rather startling suggestion is made in this memorandum signed by the auditor general, which in my judgment is not only a deviation from the established customs and practice in connection with the reporting to the people of Canada on the expenditures of the government. but which I am inclined to think is a violation of the statute. That may be wrong; I would have to examine the proposals with much greater care in order to substantiate a suggestion or statement of that character. But if this sort of thing is to happen; if a committee consisting of the auditor general, the deputy minister of finance and the comptroller of the treasury meet and put their heads together, no matter how good their intent may be from the point of view of the administration of accounting, what mandate have they from the House of Commons to dig into this thing at all and set at defiance the spirit of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act? It may be necessary to do this thing. I do not think it is necessary, but if so it should be done by parliament under the leadership of the Minister of Finance and the government. These gentlemen may have very high standing; I have great regard for the two whom I know, but I say they are travelling outside their jurisdiction when they make these suggestions which in effect would
overrule the true intent and meaning of a statute relating to this matter which was passed by parliament in 1931 and which has been lived up to by all governments and auditors general since that time.
In brief the auditor general suggests an altogether new set-up. This memoranda apparently was written in March, 1942, and in it he states:
On March 27 last I addressed a letter jointly to the deputy minister of finance and the comptroller of the treasury.
He goes on to refer to a statement made by the Prime Minister outlining the manpower policies to be applied forthwith to promote the total war effort, and says that the intent is to avoid labour wastage, and so on. That is the preliminary text, and I assume that the auditor general has in mind that he is going to eliminate the use of some manpower in the preparation of this report. Further down, in the middle of page 636, he says:
My thought is: A document called the public accounts. Part I would present the financial operations and transactions of the year, as submitted to the minister by the deputy minister of finance, who might personally contribute only the survey of the financial operations-along the lines of his present introductory statement to the balance sheet. The comptroller of the treasury would compile the statements of operations in such detail as the governor in council directs. The state of the several accounts would be certified by him-
That is, the comptroller of the treasury, though by statute that is the duty of the auditor general.
and by the auditor general. Part II would be prepared and signed by the auditor general and be his report to the house. It ivould comprise such comments as he considers necessary on matters recorded in Part I and such observations and reports as other statutory directions might require.
If hon. members will read the whole statement I am sure they will be astonished at what is in effect a suggestion to his collaborators, the deputy minister of finance and the comptroller of t.he treasury, that the act of this parliament in regard to public accounts be defied, as well as the directions contained in the whole of part V of the audit act. I must say that I was astounded when I read this part of the auditor general's report. I am not in a position to say whether the suggestion made by the auditor general would be an improvement or otherwise under the present set-up, but I am rather struck with the curious indifference on the part of those responsible for these suggestions toward those most intimately concerned with their results;

that is, the members of the House of Commons. There is nowhere in this report any suggestion that these proposed changes should be referred to the House of Commons or the members of the house. Well, have we attained that degree of bureaucracy in Canada when our accounting officials simply ignore the House of Commons? That is the way it looks to me. These gentlemen, irrespective of custom, sanction, usage and the law itself, are setting up a new programme which they think will be better. I have no doubt they hold this opinion honestly; I am not questioning the sincerity of their motives at all.
It is one of the new dangers.
Absolutely; it is a part of the new tyranny. It is a clear indication of the new bureaucracy that is to run this country in the days that are to come.

The minister need not worry himself about my injuring myself. I am quite capable of taking care of myself. But I am asking him if the statement he made on July 31 last was not made in the dying days of the session, that most people did not understand what it was all about, and that he never asked for the concurrence of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member is attacking the new one now; he attacked the old one last year.

I wish to have the House of Commons retain control of the auditor general's report, and how it shall be presented to the house; I do not wish to have that control in a bureaucracy. Is that a principle worth contending for? Is it, or is it not? I ask each hon. member in the committee to question himself this way: does he understand the auditor general's report? We are not all chartered accountants; we are not all keen-eyed lawyers; we are not all great students. But if, when looking over the public accounts, we see something which we think looks improper, we like to see it in the bright light of day, and then we can make our inquiries about it. Go into this auditor general's report; look at any account you like, and tell me, if you can, where the money has gone. It just cannot be done, and hon. members know it. In their hearts they will all agree with me, whether or not they rise in their places and help me in what I am trying to do.
I have indicated that for sixty years at least the house has been accustomed to receive information with regard to revenues and expenditures from its own special officer, the auditor general. That officer, in the words of the statute, is appointed:
. . . for the more complete examination of the accounts of Canada and for the reporting thereon to the House of Commons.
That is the fundamental principle of his duty. And, as if to make it clear beyond any doubt that reporting by the auditor general, and not mere certification of accounts and statements prepared by someone else is required, we enacted section 41 of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act commanding him to report annually to the House of Commons the result of his examination, in such manner as will exhibit the true state of each account at the termination of the fiscal year last ended.
Does anybody say that this bluebook I hold in my hand fulfils that qualification, or that direction or command, in law? Notwithstanding the fundamentals of this situation, three civil servants, high civil servants in the confidence of the government, and I think high

Interim Supply Bill
in the confidence of the country-I am bound to say thaC-have taken it upon themselves- and I do not know whether they have done so with the direction of the Minister of Finance- to advise the minister that he should change the whole course of public accounting.
I am calling attention to this situation, and I hope the committee will take heed of what I say. The effect of the situation is that the statutory obligations of the official in charge by this recommendation is informing the house that the statutory requirements are to be ignored, and that a totally new formula of reporting is being put into effect. That is the effect of the recommendation. An over-all statement of financial affairs will be furnished by the deputy minister of finance; a detailed statement of revenues and expenditures will be prepared by the comptroller of the treasury, and the auditor general will confine his reporting to such comments as he considers it necessary to impart to the house.
Is that the conception we have of the Auditor General of Canada? Is that our conception of the functions of the Auditor General of Canada, at a time when our peace-time budget has risen to over $600,000,000, the highest in the history of our country, and at a time when our war-time budget has reached an aggregate figure of around five billions of dollars? I do not think it is. I do not think the country understands the import of these things.
These changes, as I indicated, are drastic, but they may be wholly desirable. I should like to feel they were not based upon mere bureaucracy. They may be wholly desirable. But, Mr. Chairman, and members of the committee, these changes are being made by the wrong people. They should be made by the people's representatives, but once more parliamentary government is being thrown into the discard, and we are being told by a committee of highly placed civil servants how we should handle the public accounts of the country. I think that is wrong. I suggest to the minister himself that that is wrong.
The House of Commons, and it only, has the right to say in what manner it is to receive the information it desires to receive, and which the statute commands it shall receive.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Upon what section does the hon. member rely?

I rely upon the whole of the sections, and particularly upon section 49.
I suggest to the minister with the best of good feeling that it is not part of the duties of the executive, or of the deputies of executive, to arrange such matters. The auditor
general has no right of decision in the matter. And if after sixty years the house has been satisfied to receive financial statements in detail from the auditor general, it is that officer's duty so to satisfy his masters. When after many years the legislature thought it desirable to embody in the statute the specific direction of section 49, it seems clear to me that the auditor general would be grievously at fault if, without specific instructions from the house, he proceeded in any other manner.
That is the position. Of course, if the exigencies of war or any other circumstances should make it necessary to change the formula of reporting, and to waive the relative express statutory provisions, it should be done after due deliberation of the house, and not upon the ipse dixit of the Minister of Finance on July 31 last, or that of a committee of his civil servants. It should be done by the House of Commons.
That is the plea I make to-night, that this is a matter within the jurisdiction of the House of Commons itself, and that it is not an executive function.
The hon. member should speak louder.
I do not know; perhaps I am speaking too loudly, but I feel rather strongly about the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does it not all depend upon whether it is in accordance with the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act?

Yes; but I suggest that the interpretation I have given is the true interpretation. It is based on sixty years history and experience and the previous legislation out of which this arose. Section 49 was amended when this statute was put through. It was in the old revised statutes. It was expressly strengthened when the new Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act was put through. I suggest to the minister; I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, and I suggest to the membership of the committee that the intention was tq strengthen the position of the auditor general with respect to reporting the public accounts of the country. Now that is to be thrown into the discard.
I suggest to the minister that this should be done only after due consideration by the house, either in a full-dress debate in which the proposals are formally laid before parliament or after they have been examined into by a committee of this House of Commons. That is one of their prerogatives, to know how they shall receive their accounts. It is not an executive function. The committee should report pro or con to the house, if the

matter is submitted to a committee. Whether it is done in the house by means of a full-dress debate or by means of a report of a committee, in either case it should be done only by legislation following that action.
The house is supreme in matters of finance. That is a fundamental principle. It follows as day follows night that the House of Commons, if supreme in matters of finance, has the right to say how the finance shall be accounted to it. That is a corollary arising out of the primary principle I have enunciated. I was greatly surprised to hear that the primary mover in this matter is the auditor general for whom, I reiterate, I have the most friendly feelings and the highest personal regard. Last year the report of the auditor general was criticized, and I recall quite well the statement made by the minister as a result of that criticism. On July 31, the one hundred and twenty-second day of the session, when everyone was struggling to get through with the business of the house, the minister made a long statement which takes up two pages of Hansard, after which some debate in committee followed. I think the hon. member for Davenport was the only other hon. member who spoke. I do not recall whether I was in the house at the time.
I think the hon. member for Temiscouata also spoke.

I cannot see his name on the record. It must have been one of those occasions when he was absent. The minister reviewed the situation, but he did not refer to the legal position and the binding obligation, as I see it, of the statute upon which this report is based. Section 49 and the preceding sections are the whole basis to-day of the auditor general's report. It has always been governed by statute. It is not a matter of custom; it is not a question of the permanent officials of the treasury being able to do thus and so as they please; it is a matter of statutory duty and direction. I suggest that that is being ignored.	.
So far as the report that has come to my attention is concerned, the suggestion is that this emanates from the auditor general. Is it a fair inference that the proposed formula of reporting, instigated so far as the printed record would show by the auditor general himself, is a device designed to avoid further criticism or at least to deflect it elsewhere? The suggestion that it stems from a desire to meet man-power policy outlined by the government is, I suggest, wholly specious.

If you will inquire at the civil service commission, I think you will find that the information is forthcoming that pursuant to representations made by the auditor general, or at least emanating from the auditor general, steps are almost completed for bringing into his office a considerable number of new highly paid employees to take the place of the slightly greater number of less highly paid employees who have been transferred to the office of the comptroller of the treasury,, allegedly to enable that officer to produce the detailed report contemplated by the new formula.
Under this proposal a number of high officers will be transferred to the comptroller of the treasury, and there will be. taken into the auditor general's department a substantial number-I do not know how many- of highly paid men to take their places. There will be no saving of man-power or man-power hours in that regard. I ask the minister if that is true. I know it must stand to reason that as a result of the great increase in the volume of business there must be increased work in the departments of the auditor general and the comptroller of the treasury. The telephone list will show that treasury officers are everywhere in Ottawa. They should be.
There must be treasury control. I have never suggested any other principle. Some people think that perhaps there is too much treasury control, but I suggest that there cannot be when you are spending S5.000,-000,000, half of which is being obtained in taxation and the other half by borrowings from the people. This is the proper system, and it should be carried out to the nth degree. I wish there was as much control in letting contracts as there is in checking contracts. So far as I understand the situation, the treasury control officers have done pretty good work. The complaints I have received are that they are not liberal enough in allowances for salary and what-not. When these gentlemen wdth contracts come to see me I ask them what they are complaining about. I tell them if they make a lot of money .they will have to pay it back in taxes and they might as well work for the government. We are all working for the government until this war is over. The whole country is working for the government, and why not?

The government is
working for the country.

The government is working for the country, but I will say that the country's effort is greater than the government's effort and it has been from

the beginning. The country has always been ahead of this government, and it is ahead today. What happened on Saturday only emphasizes what the country is willing to do in our sphere of human activity. I did' not intend to bring up this matter to-night, but this is the first opportunity I have to do so since I read that suggestion of the auditor general in the general observations under the head of "revenue and expenditure reporting". I should like hon. members to give some thought to these things. This is one occasion upon which members can impress their ideas upon the minister with regard to how public accounts should be made up and how they should be put before the public so that we may know where the money goes. I do not think they are. I think they are part of the ordinary food of the people of this country.
The government could have taken three courses with respect to the importation of these articles. They could have disregarded the price ceiling and let the prices of them rise to such level as the market might drive prices to. That would in effect be the piercing of the price ceiling and would be undesirable from that point of view.
They rose anyway, did they not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
I paid as high as ninety cents a dozen for oranges.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The second course the government could have taken would have been to maintain the price ceiling in respect of these articles, in which event importations would have ceased, because they could not be brought in and sold under the price ceiling owing to their increased cost abroad. The third thing the government could have done was to pay subsidies, as they did, treating the loss as merely a species of subsidy.

He is an appointee, an official of the parliament of Canada. He is an officer of parliament. The statements referred to in this section shall include

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think so. His duties are all covered before, and nothing is added except that it must exhibit the true state of each account at the end of the fiscal year just ended. He cannot leave it up to some previous period. That is what it means. As to what it was proposed to do, I ask hon. members to read the speech I made on this subject on July 31 last, after a very full consideration of the subject. The comptroller of the treasury prepares the public accounts for the deputy minister of finance to sign, and it was proposed to let him cover the whole field very fully and make a full presentation of the expenditures of the government for the fiscal year in question. Hon. members will find in that speech the degree of itemization which I considered desirable, and the suggestion that the auditor general, instead of doing the same thing over again and thereby effecting a duplication, which is entirely unnecessary, should in the same volume, within one cover, append his certificate to these accounts, referring to the accounts, complying with the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act in respect of those accounts that are presented by the auditor general, and making such comments upon them as he thought fit.
The hon. gentleman has raised a legal question. He says this violates certain sections of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, and if he wishes me to do so I will refer the question to the Department of Justice to ascertain whether there is anything in his legal point. It never occurred to anyone that there was. In the speech to which I have referred, I said:
In the course of our consideration we have studied not only the law and the historical background relating to the reports to parliament on government revenues and expenditures, assets and liabilities, et cetera, in so far as Canada is concerned, but also the practices followed by the United States, the United Kingdom, and the other British dominions. Our desire was to draw from all possible sources lessons and suggestions as to the best possible way in which to present to parliament the information necessary to enable it to exercise wisely and efficiently its control over financial matters and assure itself that the executive arm of government is properly carrying out its stewardship. As a result of the study and consideration given to the whole matter, .1 am glad to be able to announce that the government has decided to accept certain recommendations made jointly by the auditor general, the deputy minister of finance, and the comptroller of the treasury. The government believes that these recommendations are sound, and, if they commend themselves to the judgment of the house, they will he implemented with respect to the accounts for the current fiscal year.
I may pause here to point out that the profession of the auditor general is not that of an accountant. He is a barrister and solicitor, and he has a pronounced legal approach to the discharge of his duties. The reference here to the study of the law and of the historical background relating to reports to parliament on government revenues and expenditures, in so far as Canada is concerned, as well as the United States, and so on, is a reference to the consideration which this able lawyer, the auditor general, has given to the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, which I presume he had some part in drafting. I presume he had. He was a prominent official in the Department of Finance at the time the new Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act was drafted, and therefore this recommendation is no flighty or hasty notion of men who do not know what they are doing. They are men who have legal background, financial background, historical background, men who have appreciation of the constitutional responsibilities of the government and of the auditor general to parliament.

But not of the rights of parliament.
Mr. II.SLEY: I think so. If the hon. gentleman thinks there is anything in his legal point, I will refer it to the Department of Justice and perhaps we can change this system if we find it is not a legal system. Or perhaps we should amend the law to validate or ratify what we are doing; for I venture to say that if, instead of doing as the hon. gentleman did to-night in bringing so much heat and so little light to a consideration of this question; if, instead of saying, as he said to-night, "I do not know whether it is a good thing to do or not, but certainly I do not like the way in which it is done," hon. members would get their minds down to whether or not it is a good thing to do, they would come to the conclusion that what we are doing is a good thing. This is something of which he complains in the foreword of his report. He said, "How can I give a report? There are no vouchers, and they refuse to give me a voucher." This is a serious matter; and in this regard we are not complaining at all about the auditor general. I think all hon. members should stand by him when he mentions things like that. It is not only in defence <jf the auditor general that I speak in this way; it is for the protection of the Minister of Finance and the defence of the government at large, and for the prevention of abuses by those civil servants and others who take advantage of the darkness to pass things over the heads of members of parliament.
In this matter we have nothing personally against the Minister of Finance or any other minister. But we desire a reform of this system, and we want the people of the country to know what is going on here in Ottawa. There is an excuse which is given at times, to this effect, "Oh, now we are spending such large amounts of money." That is not a reason at all for not adhering to the old method of accounting which was good when we were spending ten times less then than we are doing now. Of course the departments grow larger and larger, but the size of the expenditures is no reason or excuse for changing the sane and sound method of accounting which was good in the time of Laurier, Borden and others. If there is a change in accounting due to adding machines and other mechanical improvements, the fundamental system should be the same: it
should be a system of having an account of everything which is done by the government. That is the old system. There is nothing new in that. It has been done in England for centuries. Of course people in England admit that the fashion changes for certain matters, but it cannot change for this; it is the very reason we are here.
We are here for two reasons. We are here in the first place to enact legislation, and the only legislation which is submitted to us is for taxation. But we are here for a second reason, which is not less important. It is to check the expenditures. It would be impossible for members of parliament to receive all the detail which has been omitted) from these accounts; but what we want is to have some information in the regular way, to have it without asking for it by motions or otherwise and waiting months and months to get it.
Sometimes it is said that it is not in the public interest to give this or that piece of information. How is that? Where is the judge? The judges are just appointees of the government, who are there to see that members shall not put their noses in this business. But when we do so, we do it for the welfare of the government as well as for the welfare of the country.
It is not my intention to insist on this point any further to-night, but I may have something more to say in reply if there should be any more contradiction. I want the minister to understand fully what it is we ask. Our point is that we should have complete information, information to the same degree as was given by the union government during the last war. I hope that in this matter this government will at feast act as wisely as the union government did in those times. '

I can say what I have to say in one minute. The minister would like to know what it is I am asking for. The second part of the auditor general's report for 1939 alone contained about twelve hundred pages; the auditor general's report for 1942 has six hundred and thirty-eight pages. I always like to look through the record of the Department of Mines aijd Resources, and I observe that in the current report that department is covered in twenty-six pages, whereas in 1939 there were one hundred and twenty-six pages. I am also especially interested in the figures relating to the Indian affairs branch. I find that in the 1942 report everything relating to Indian affairs is given in eleven lines, whereas in 1939 there are thirty-eight pages. How can I find anything that I am looking for in such meagre reports as we have in 1942?
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.

Privilege-Mr. Coldwell
